title.text: Our Lady of Candelaria Parish Church (Silang)

title_en.text: Our Lady of Candelaria Parish Church (Silang)

tagline.text: Cavite's oldest stone church and its 17th-century Baroque altarpieces

location.label: Location
location.text: J. Rizal Street, town center, Silang, Cavite

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: December–May dry season (February 1–3 feast days differ)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,200 (round trip by public transport from Manila, plus meals)

children.text: This church in the heart of Silang belongs to a parish founded in 1595. The stone building was constructed in 1637–1639 and dedicated in 1640. It is regarded as the oldest stone church in Cavite, and its 17th-century Baroque altarpieces are a National Cultural Treasure.

Our Lady of Candelaria Parish Church is a Roman Catholic church on J. Rizal Street in the center of Silang, a highland town in southern Cavite. Its Spanish name is Nuestra Señora de Candelaria, and locals simply call it Silang Church. It belongs to the Diocese of Imus and is now also a Diocesan Shrine, still serving as an active parish. It is close to Tagaytay, so it is a good historic stop if you come for the views, coffee and farm cafes. Its history goes back to the 16th century. The Franciscans began evangelizing the area in the mid-1580s and formally founded Silang as a parish in 1595. At first there was only a small chapel and school built of light materials, and a fire destroyed everything on August 30, 1603. The Jesuits took over afterward, though sources differ on when, either 1599 or 1611, so it is hard to be definite. The present stone church was built by the Jesuit Fr. Juan de Salazar between 1637 and 1639 and was dedicated to Our Lady of Candelaria in 1640. For this reason it is described as the oldest surviving stone church in Cavite.

The building is in a simple Baroque style. It has thick walls and buttresses, and some accounts say it also served as a refuge against bandits in the old days. According to the National Museum, the church has a cruciform plan with the nave running north to south, so the altar is at the north end and the main portal faces south. The facade is a modest pedimented front divided by moldings and pilasters, with a round-arched portal on the ground level and, above it, two windows and a niche holding the statue of Our Lady of Candelaria. One story explains the plain facade by saying that Fr. Salazar died in 1640. The bell tower stands on the east side and has four stories; the fourth collapsed in the 1880 earthquake and was restored in 1989. The two-story convent is attached to the northeast of the church.

The real reason to come is the altarpieces inside. Three retablos, the main altar and two side altars, were made between 1643 and 1663 as wooden works in Baroque style with Rococo touches. The main retablo tells the life of Mary like a picture book based on the mysteries of the Rosary, and the image of Our Lady of Candelaria sits in its central niche. The side altars are described as depicting women saints on the gospel side and Jesuit saints on the epistle side. Look for local Philippine motifs such as plants, fruit and even millipedes carved into the designs. You can see colonial-era art up close, where European forms meet the hands of local craftsmen. The National Museum declared these altarpieces a National Cultural Treasure, though sources disagree on whether the year was 2016 or 2017.

The star of the church is Our Lady of Candelaria. According to tradition, a native named Andres found the image in 1640; it kept disappearing until a Jesuit rector advised bringing it to the church, and after that it stayed. Her feast day is February 2, and Silang holds a procession and festival every year from February 1 to 3. The National Historical Commission (NHCP) installed a historical marker at the church in 2008. This is not a crowded tourist attraction but a living church where residents still attend Mass, so plan to sit quietly and look up at the altar for a while. Some accounts also mention that the community published a heritage book about the church, In Nomine, in 2018, so if you are interested in history, you could ask whether it is available locally. Since 1978 the parish has been run by diocesan priests; before that, the National Museum notes, it passed among several orders and clergy, including the Franciscans, Jesuits, secular priests, Augustinian Recollects and Columbans. Keep in mind that traces of many eras overlap in this one building as you look around.
Built in 1637–1639 and dedicated in 1640, it is described as the oldest surviving stone church in Cavite province. After nearly 400 years, it has kept its basic form through earthquakes and wars.
The main altar and two side altars, made in 1643–1663, fill the church. Gilded columns, floral patterns and images of saints stand in contrast to the modest facade.

blocks.title: A main altar that tells Mary's life

children.text: The main altar shows the life of Mary in relief based on the mysteries of the Rosary. The statue of Our Lady of Candelaria stands in the central niche, drawing the eye naturally.

blocks.title: Local motifs of millipedes and fruit

children.text: The altar decoration is said to include local motifs such as plants, fruit and millipedes. It is fun to look for traces of Philippine craftsmen's touch within the European style.

The facade is neatly divided by moldings and pilasters, with the statue of Our Lady in a niche on the upper level. With no elaborate carving, the thick walls and buttresses give it a fortress-like look.

The bell tower on the east side has four stories; the fourth collapsed in the 1880 earthquake and was restored in 1989. A two-story convent is attached to the northeast, showing how the church complex is laid out.

blocks.title: NHCP marker and National Cultural Treasure

children.text: The National Historical Commission installed a marker in 2008, and the altarpieces were declared a National Cultural Treasure. Check the marker's location and wording on site.

A procession and festival take place around the feast of Our Lady of Candelaria on February 2. You can see local faith culture up close, but it is much more crowded than usual, so check the schedule in advance.

items.title: Half-day route combined with Tagaytay
items.subtitle: Church visit and a walk around Silang town

children.text: Travel from Tagaytay to the church on J. Rizal Street in central Silang. Transport options depend on local conditions, so ask a ride-hailing app or driver.
First look at the facade, the statue of Our Lady in the upper niche and the east bell tower from the churchyard. If it is a Sunday Mass hour, wait until the Mass ends.
Step quietly inside and look at the reliefs and motifs of the main altar and the side altars one by one. Feel the cool air created by the high ceiling and thick walls.
Walk around the NHCP marker and the plaza area, and have a simple lunch at a town restaurant or street stall.
Head back to Tagaytay and continue to a viewpoint or cafe.
The church is a place where believers pray, so please mind your clothing and noise. All times are examples only.
A common way is to take a bus from Manila (Pasay, Cubao and elsewhere) to Tagaytay and then transfer toward Silang. Routes, fares and departure terminals change often, so check locally.
With a private car or a ride-hailing app, you can go directly toward the Aguinaldo Highway. Travel time from Manila varies greatly with traffic, so allow plenty of time.
A route leaving CAVITEX and following the Aguinaldo Highway appears in guide materials. Still, rely on your map app's route.
The church is on J. Rizal Street in central Silang; search for Our Lady of Candelaria Parish Church in a map app to find it.
You can walk around town, and for longer distances use a tricycle or a ride-hailing app.

Indoor viewing is the main activity, so the season matters little, but the dry season is more comfortable because the approach is outdoors. Silang is in the highlands and cooler than Manila, so walking around is easy even by day.

The February 1–3 Candelaria festival brings processions and events and gets crowded, and believers also flock to the church during Holy Week and at Christmas. Weekday mornings are best if you want to see the altar quietly. Check the latest announcements for Mass times.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Best for viewing and strolling; the festival takes place in early February.
Avoid midday and visit in the morning.
Bring an umbrella and leave slack in your schedule.

Silang town has small restaurants and street stalls where you can easily have a simple lunch. The area is also known for farms and coffee plantations, so you can stop at a nearby cafe after the church. Business names change often, so check recent reviews on a map app.
Hotels and resorts are more varied on the Tagaytay side. For a day trip, a sensible plan is to stay in Tagaytay and visit Silang church as a half-day trip.

Seeing the church itself takes only an hour or two, so rather than lingering in Silang, we recommend linking it with Tagaytay's viewpoints, cafes and farm experiences. Try snacks from local stalls with an eye on hygiene and price, and ask first where prices are not fixed.
The facade is modest, so lower your expectations and go to see the altar. The retablos inside are the highlight.
Modest clothing that covers shoulders and knees is best.
Avoid photography and moving around during Mass, and avoid Mass hours. Some sources list several Sunday Masses in the morning and late afternoon, but check the latest announcements.
Be careful with flash and tripods. The wooden carvings of the altars are old cultural property.
During the February 1–3 festival, go early or choose another day.
It is efficient to combine it with a Tagaytay itinerary. Making a long trip just to see this one church is not worth the time.
Traffic is heavy on this route, so leave plenty of time for the return.
This is an active church, so do not disturb Mass or prayer, and watch your belongings in town.
Mass times and opening hours can change, so check the parish or diocese announcements before you go.
Crowds gather during the festival, so keep your phone and wallet in front of you.
Transport fares and routes change often, so check locally.
Sources differ on the year the altarpieces were declared a cultural treasure (2016 or 2017) and on when the Jesuits took over, so we have not stated either definitively.
Avoid traveling late at night and use a ride-hailing car instead.
A nearby highland resort town famous for Taal Lake views and cafes. Travel time varies with traffic, so check locally.
A viewpoint park on the Tagaytay side. Try combining it with the church visit in one itinerary.

blocks.title: National Shrine of Our Lady of La Salette

children.text: According to sources, it is a shrine in Biga II in the same town of Silang, on the Aguinaldo Highway, so it is easy to stop at on the way to Tagaytay.
